author: Mike Michalowicz
refresher: The formula changes the budgeting order, not accounting arithmetic. Reserve a deliberate profit amount, then design operations around the remaining cash while meeting existing obligations.

author: Mike Michalowicz
concept: Give each dollar a separate purpose
quote: Each of these accounts has a differ ent objective: one is for profit, one for owner compensation, another for taxes and another for operating expenses.
refresher: The small-plates system separates cash for profit, owner pay, taxes, and operating costs. The operating balance becomes a spending boundary; the total bank balance is not all available to spend.

author: Mike Michalowicz
quote: Move your PROFIT account and other "tempting" accounts out of arm's reach.
refresher: Separate reserves from everyday spending so an impulsive decision requires an extra step. Keep necessary access for genuine obligations; friction is a behavioral aid, not a substitute for cash planning.

links.title: CFPB · Where to keep dedicated savings

author: Mike Michalowicz
concept: Give cash allocation a recurring rhythm
quote: Enforce a Rhythm: Do your allocations and payables twice a month (specifically, on the tenth and twenty-fifth). Don't pay only when there is money piled up in the account.
refresher: A fixed review schedule makes allocation a routine instead of a response to a large balance. The book chooses twice monthly; coordinate the actual schedule with payroll, bills, and tax deadlines.

links.title: BDC · Budget and monitor cash flow

author: Mike Michalowicz
concept: Move from current allocations toward targets
quote: TAPs are not your starting point; TAPs are the targets you are moving toward. (Take them from the following table)
refresher: First measure where cash actually goes. Adjust allocations gradually and review affordability instead of immediately imposing the book’s target percentages on a business with different obligations.

author: Mike Michalowicz
concept: Separate owner labor from ownership returns
quote: Don't confuse the profit distribution with Owner's Comp, which is pay for working in the business. Profit is a reward for owning the business.
refresher: Owner compensation recognizes work performed; profit distributions recognize ownership. Keeping them distinct exposes a business that appears profitable only because its owner works unpaid. Actual payment and tax treatment depend on the business structure.

author: Mike Michalowicz
concept: Reserve tax money before it becomes a surprise
quote: So don't steal from your TAX account, thinking you won't need that money for taxes.
refresher: Tax reserves are earmarked obligations, not spare operating cash. Estimate them from the business’s actual tax position and payment dates; a generic percentage in a book cannot determine the amount owed.

author: Mike Michalowicz
concept: Retain a buffer instead of distributing everything
quote: As your profits accumulate in your PROFIT account, and you only take 50 percent as a profit distribution, the remainder will act as a rainy-day fund.
refresher: The book’s half-distribution rule deliberately leaves a reserve. The transferable principle is to keep liquidity for interruptions; the appropriate buffer depends on costs, volatility, and access to funding.

links.title: BDC · Reserves for seasonal cash flow

author: Mike Michalowicz
concept: Do not budget from your best month
quote: The trap we fall into is believing our most recent best month is our new normal. Then we start running the business according to that "normal.”
refresher: Separate a temporary sales spike from sustainable earning capacity. Compare similar seasons and use rolling history plus a forward cash forecast before taking on recurring costs.
